name: Yara Weber

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government, and we don't sell anything. What you tell me stays confidential, so you can give me the public version and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I buy pet food, feed and farm supplies for Hartfield Agricultural Supplies, which sells to about 250 farm shops and feed stores across three counties. Sacks of dog food, chicken feed, fencing wire, mineral blocks. I start with the weather forecast, because it moves demand, and then phone calls with the mills and suppliers. After lunch it's screens. I like that what I buy keeps farms and animals going. I don't like the weeks when the grain price swings and everyone phones me at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we'll see. I've watched a lot of new things come and go, and some stuck, like the barcode scanners. At church I'd say that I'm glad things aren't changing too fast. At work I'd say I'll try the tools when they've proved themselves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm content. My husband Klaus has his own fencing and baling business and it's steady, we own the house and have savings, and I'm four years from stopping. The thing I carry is the grain price, which makes my job stressful whatever AI does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on and use the chat tool now and then, as I do now, for drafting the odd email to a supplier. I'd keep the autumn buying plan the way I've always done it, with my own notes and the mill's price list. And I'd keep an eye on Hartfield's new stock software without relying on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Content. A bit relieved. Nothing worse than usual, which is a lot for these days.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the grain price. What does a swing like that do to your day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The grain price. Last winter wheat jumped, and every feed we make has wheat in it. I had to tell 40 shops their prices would go up in a week. A few shouted, and I understood.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you use the chat tool now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's the sort of problem no machine takes off my plate. When I phone a farm shop to say prices are going up, they need to hear a person's voice, and no machine can take that call. I'd say it's a human problem.

say: I'd say we'll **see**, since some new things stick and some don't.
I'd tell church friends I'm glad nothing moves **too fast**.
think: I'm content, with Klaus's **business** steady and the house ours.
The grain **price** stresses me whatever AI does.
do: Use the chat tool **now and then** for supplier emails.
Keep my **autumn buying plan** with my own notes.
Watch Hartfield's new stock **software** without relying on it.
feel: **Content**, a little relieved, with nothing worse than usual.
S0.quote: When I phone a farm shop to say prices are going up, they need to hear a person's voice, and no machine can take that call.
fieldNote: Yara's stress is the grain price, which exists with or without AI, but money and household are secure.
She is a **steady** adopter: tries tools when proven, uses the chat tool for emails.
Her quote shows pride in human contact when breaking bad news.

steps.text: Keep drafting supplier emails with the chat tool now and then
Build the autumn feed buying plan from my own notes

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say change is coming and the sensible thing is to handle it step by step. At church I'd say we should look out for the young ones who'll be hit first. At work I'd say let's pilot the new tool in one product line, not everything at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think about a third of my work goes to software over three years, the stock planning and price checks. Hartfield won't replace people who leave, and the orders will be placed by a program unless a person overrides them. I think I can be the person who overrides, because I know what the farms need.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask to run the pilot on the pet food range, where the sums are simplest. I'd do the vendor course, and I'd use the chat tool for the supplier comparison work. I'd also ask the owner, Mr. Brandt, to put in writing that we won't lose staff in the first two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy, mostly because it's a lot of change at once. I'd keep reminding myself I've done well at every change so far.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about at work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marta and Piet on the order desk. They answer the shops' calls and check stock, and software can do both. I'd say to them: learn the new thing now, and I'll sit with you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd ask the owner for it in writing. Why does that matter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm not sure they'd agree. A promise made in a corridor is gone by Monday, so I'd ask the owner to put in writing that nobody loses their job for two years. But I'd keep asking.

say: I'd say let's pilot the tool in **one product line**, not everything at once.
I'd say at church we should look out for the **young ones**.
think: About a **third** of my work goes to software within three years.
I can be the person who **overrides** the machine, because I know what farms need.
do: Run the **pilot** on the pet food range.
Take the vendor **course** and use the chat tool for supplier comparisons.
Ask owner Mr. Brandt for a **written** no-layoff promise.
feel: A bit **uneasy**, mostly at the amount of change at once.
S1.quote: A promise made in a corridor is gone by Monday, so I'd ask the owner to put in writing that nobody loses their job for two years.
fieldNote: Yara is steady and practical: pilot small, learn, ask for **written** assurances.
She looks out for **Marta and Piet** on the order desk.
Uneasy because her own role looks safe but the team around her may shrink.

steps.text: Run the first pilot of the new buying tool on the pet food range
Take the vendor course and use the chat tool for supplier comparisons
Ask Mr. Brandt to put a two-year no-layoff promise in writing

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say two years is too fast and nobody's ready. At church I'd say we have to look after each other, and I'd say to the government that it should help families directly. At work I'd say let's stay calm and make an honest list of who's affected.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my job is gone in two years, and Hartfield may change hands. If a machine can do all thinking work, the mills will sell straight to farm shops. That's a hard thing to say out loud after 33 years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for a package, take it and finish. Klaus and I would put his business first, so I'd do his invoices and ordering, and we'd both stay hands-on, since the machines can't build a fence for three more years. We'd cut back on spending, keep a year's cash and pay off the last of the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd find it hard to settle. I'd pray about it, and then I'd get on with a list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your children, Lena and Jonas?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our daughter Lena is a vet nurse, which is hands-on and safe for longer, and our son Jonas manages a farm, which is partly thinking work. I'd tell Jonas to learn the farm's machinery and to keep his options open. I'd tell them both that the farm is always a place to come back to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd work in Klaus's business. How would that work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The machines can think in two years but they can't build a fence for three more, so I'd go and work beside my husband. I'd rather work with my husband than wait for a letter.

say: I'd say two years is **too fast** and nobody's ready.
I'd tell the government to help **families** directly.
think: My job is **gone** in two years, and Hartfield may change hands.
The mills could sell straight to farm shops, and that's hard after **33 years**.
do: Ask for a **package**, take it and finish.
Do Klaus's **invoices** and ordering in his fencing business.
Cut spending, keep a year's **cash** and pay off the mortgage.
feel: **Anxious**, and I'd pray about it and then get on with a list.
S2.quote: The machines can think in two years but they can't build a fence for three more, so I'd go and work beside my husband.
fieldNote: Yara expects the buying job to end and quickly sees a hands-on route through her husband's business.
Her use of the **robot lag** is practical and fits her family's trades.
Faith and family are steadying, not just a comfort.

steps.text: Ask Hartfield for a package and finish
Take over the invoices and ordering for Klaus's fencing business
Pay off the last of the mortgage and keep a year's cash

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives us time to make good choices. At church we'd talk about what each family would do. At work I'd ask management to set out a plan, with dates, for the buying team.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd finish before the worst of it, at 62. I'd be safe, I think. But I'd worry about Marta and Piet, and about the farm shops, who'll lose some of the service that they depend on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work three more years and use them to learn the tools properly. I'd train Marta to take over the supplier calls. I'd start putting my notes into a guide so that Hartfield doesn't lose what I know. And I'd bring Klaus's invoicing onto a simple program.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with a plan. It's a good feeling to have a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would be in the guide you mentioned?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd write the guide in plain words: which mill delivers late in January, which farm shops pay slowly, who needs a call before the price rises. I'd give a copy to Marta and keep one for myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask management for in the plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A written guide to which mill is late in January and which farm shop pays slowly is worth more than any manual the software comes with. I'd feel better if I knew it would help someone.

say: I'd say five years gives us time to make good **choices**.
I'd ask management for a **plan with dates** for the buying team.
think: I'd finish at **62**, before the worst of it.
I'd worry about **Marta and Piet** and the farm shops' service.
do: Work **three more years** and learn the tools properly.
Train **Marta** to take over supplier calls.
Write a plain-words **guide** to what I know.
feel: **Anxious**, but better for having a plan.
S3.quote: A written guide to which mill is late in January and which farm shop pays slowly is worth more than any manual the software comes with.
fieldNote: Yara plans to pass on her knowledge through a written guide and training Marta.
The five years let her feel in control, yet she stays **anxious** about her colleagues and the shops.
Traditional values show: duty to colleagues and to farm customers.

steps.text: Work three more years and learn the buying tools properly
Train Marta to take over supplier calls
Put Klaus's invoicing onto a simple program

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, and the world may look different by then. At church I'd say keep faith and teach your children to work. At work I'd say let's keep learning, a little at a time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it won't touch me, as I'll have been home for six years. I'd be calm for myself, uneasy for my grandchildren, when I have them, and for the people in town who'll face this later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work until 62 and then help Klaus in his business, and I'd volunteer at the church food bank. I'd put some savings aside for the children's training. And I'd keep trying new tools at my own pace.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Quite calm. It feels like a distant harvest: you plan for it, but you don't lose sleep over it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your children, Lena and Jonas?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Lena: you've got a hands-on job, but keep learning. I'd tell Jonas: farms will use more machines, so be the man who knows how they work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do at the food bank?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is like a distant harvest: you plan for it and prepare, but you don't lose sleep over it. We'd talk it through at the Sunday lunch table.

say: I'd say ten years is a long time and the world may **look different**.
I'd say at church to keep faith and teach children to **work**.
think: It won't touch me, since I'll have been **home for six years**.
I'm uneasy for **grandchildren** and for the town.
do: Work until **62**, then help Klaus in his business.
Put savings aside for the children's **training**.
S4.quote: Ten years is like a distant harvest: you plan for it and prepare, but you don't lose sleep over it.
fieldNote: At ten years Yara's unease is for the next generation and the town.
Her **harvest** image fits her farm-supply world.
Her plans are about service and family, not her own job.

steps.text: Work until 62, then help Klaus in his fencing business
Put savings aside for Lena's and Jonas's training
Volunteer at the church food bank

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. Nobody's ready, not the shops, not the farms, not the church or the council. What would help is time, fair treatment of people who leave, and help for small towns that lose their jobs together.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only one thing. I'll try anything once it's been proven, but I won't throw out thirty years of knowing farms to please a program.

headlineQuote: I'll try anything once it's been proven, but I won't throw out thirty years of knowing farms to please a program.
portrait: Yara is **58**, a feed and farm-supplies buyer at Hartfield Agricultural Supplies, who uses AI tools now and then.
She's traditional and church-going, steady and practical, preferring to **pilot** things and write guides.
Her husband Klaus's fencing business and a paid-off house keep her calm when change is slow.
In the fast worlds she's anxious, takes a **package** and joins Klaus's hands-on business.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** world, because no shop, farm, church or council is ready.
whatWouldHelp: **Time**, fair treatment for people who leave and help for small towns.
